summary: Midodrine is an oral prodrug that is deglycinated to desglymidodrine, a peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that raises arteriolar and venous tone to increase standing blood pressure. It is indicated for symptomatic orthostatic hypotension in patients whose lives are considerably impaired despite standard care. Its most serious risk is marked supine hypertension (systolic >200 mmHg in some patients), which is the subject of a boxed warning. To minimize nighttime supine hypertension, doses are given only during daytime upright hours, with the last dose no later than 6 P.M. and never within 4 hours of lying down. Approval rests on a surrogate marker (1-minute standing systolic pressure), and treatment should be continued only in patients with clear symptomatic improvement.
indications: Treatment of symptomatic orthostatic hypotension in patients whose lives are considerably impaired despite standard clinical care (support stockings, fluid expansion, lifestyle measures)

moa: Midodrine is a prodrug with little intrinsic activity; after rapid oral absorption it is deglycinated to desglymidodrine, the active alpha-1 adrenergic agonist. Desglymidodrine activates alpha-1 receptors on arteriolar and venous smooth muscle, increasing peripheral vascular tone and raising standing, sitting, and supine blood pressure. It does not stimulate cardiac beta-adrenergic receptors and crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, so it lacks direct cardiac stimulation and central nervous system effects. A 10 mg dose raises standing systolic pressure by roughly 15 to 30 mmHg at 1 hour, with some effect persisting 2 to 3 hours; a slight reflex vagal slowing of heart rate may occur.

Standing blood pressure and symptomatic response

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. In animals, midodrine increased embryo resorption, reduced fetal body weight in rats and rabbits, and decreased fetal survival in rabbits at 13 (rat) and 7 (rabbit) times the maximum human dose on a body-surface-area basis, though no teratogenic effects were observed. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether midodrine is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk, exercise caution when administering midodrine to a nursing woman.
renal: Midodrine has not been studied in patients with renal impairment. Because desglymidodrine is eliminated renally (renal clearance ~385 mL/min, ~80% by active tubular secretion), higher blood levels are expected in renal impairment; use with caution and initiate at 2.5 mg. Assess renal function before starting therapy. Acute renal disease is a contraindication. Desglymidodrine is removed by hemodialysis.
hepatic: Midodrine has not been studied in patients with hepatic impairment. Because the liver has a role in the metabolism of midodrine, use with caution and assess hepatic function before and during therapy as appropriate.

major: MAO inhibitors or linezolid - avoid concomitant use
Drugs that raise blood pressure (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, dihydroergotamine, thyroid hormones, droxidopa) - increased hypertension risk; avoid, or monitor BP closely if unavoidable
Cardiac glycosides (e.g., digitalis) - may enhance or precipitate bradycardia, AV block, or arrhythmia
moderate: Beta blockers, psychopharmacologic agents, and other heart-rate-lowering drugs - additive bradycardia risk
Salt-retaining steroids (fludrocortisone acetate, with/without salt) - supine hypertension risk; may need lower fludrocortisone dose or reduced salt intake
Alpha-adrenergic blockers (prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin) - antagonize midodrine effect
Drugs sharing the renal base-secreting pathway (metformin, cimetidine, ranitidine, procainamide, triamterene, flecainide, quinidine) - potential interaction
minor: Over-the-counter cold remedies and diet aids - may potentiate pressor effects; use cautiously
interactions.food: Food does not affect the bioavailability of the active metabolite desglymidodrine; however, do not dose after the evening meal.
interactions.alcohol: Use alcohol cautiously; it may aggravate orthostatic symptoms.
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory interference reported; assess renal and hepatic function before and during treatment.

Reflex bradycardia / AV block (especially with cardiac glycosides)
emergency: Hypertensive crisis with supine hypertension increasing stroke/cardiovascular event risk

Standing blood pressure and symptomatic improvement to justify continued use

counsel: Take this medicine only during the daytime when you will be up and about; never take it at bedtime
Take your last dose 3 to 4 hours before lying down and no later than 6 P.M. - do not dose within 4 hours of lying down
Do not lie flat for a few hours after a dose; elevate the head of your bed at night to lower the risk of high blood pressure while lying down
Report at once: pounding in the ears, headache, blurred vision, or cardiac awareness - these may signal supine high blood pressure; stop the drug if it persists
Avoid over-the-counter cold remedies and diet aids, which can raise blood pressure
Tell your doctor about slowing pulse, increasing dizziness, or fainting (possible slow heart rate)
pk: Standing systolic BP rises within ~1 hour of a 10 mg dose
Desglymidodrine peaks ~1 to 2 hours after dosing (prodrug peaks ~0.5 hour)
Pressor effect persists about 2 to 3 hours; dosed three times daily
Store at 25 C (77 F); excursions permitted 15-30 C
pearls: Boxed warning: midodrine causes marked supine hypertension - monitor supine and sitting BP, not just standing BP
Prodrug - clinical effect is from the active alpha-1 agonist metabolite desglymidodrine
Never dose at bedtime or within 4 hours of lying down; last dose no later than 6 P.M.
Approval is based on a surrogate marker (1-minute standing systolic BP); continue only if real symptomatic benefit
Start at 2.5 mg and use caution in renal impairment; desglymidodrine is renally cleared and is dialyzable
Reverse pressor/overdose effects with an alpha-blocker such as phentolamine
missed: If you miss a daytime dose, take it as soon as you remember while still upright for the day; skip it if it is late in the day (within 4 hours of bedtime or after 6 P.M.) to avoid high blood pressure while lying down. Do not take a double dose and never take a dose at night to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose may cause hypertension, piloerection (goosebumps), a sensation of coldness, urinary retention, and reflex bradycardia. Treatment, based on the drug's pharmacology, includes induced emesis and administration of an alpha-sympatholytic agent (e.g., phentolamine); reported cases responded to IV phentolamine 20 mg and supportive care. Desglymidodrine is dialyzable.
